name: Deconvolution Trace Detection
description: Detects traces of deconvolution/sharpening applied to mask generation artifacts (Cho & Lee, 2009).
mechanism:
This method identifies traces left by deconvolution (blind deblurring) algorithms, which may be applied to sharpen AI-generated images or conceal generation artifacts:

1. **Ringing Artifact Detection**: Non-blind deconvolution using Wiener or Richardson-Lucy filters produces characteristic ringing (Gibbs) artifacts near high-contrast edges. The method applies a Canny edge detector followed by a 1D Fourier analysis perpendicular to each edge, detecting periodic oscillations with periods of 3–8 pixels that signify ringing.

2. **Noise Amplification Pattern**: Deconvolution amplifies high-frequency noise in a pattern determined by the inverse of the point spread function (PSF). The method estimates the noise power spectral density (PSD) and checks whether it follows the expected 1/|H(f)|² amplification pattern, where H(f) is the estimated blur kernel's frequency response.

3. **Kernel Estimation Residual**: Using the blind deconvolution approach of Cho & Lee (2009), the method estimates the most likely blur kernel from the image. If the image was deconvolved, the re-estimated kernel will be close to a delta function. The method computes the L2 distance between the estimated kernel and δ(x,y) — distances below 0.1 indicate deconvolution was applied.

4. **Spectral Flatness Analysis**: Deconvolved images show unnaturally flat power spectra in mid-to-high frequencies compared to natural images, which follow an approximate 1/f² falloff. The spectral flatness measure (geometric mean / arithmetic mean of power spectrum) above 0.4 in the 0.3–0.8 Nyquist range flags deconvolution processing.
parameters:
Edge detection: Canny with σ = 1.5
Ringing period range: 3–8 pixels
Kernel estimation size: up to 35×35 pixels
Spectral flatness threshold: 0.4
Noise PSD estimation: Welch method with 64-sample windows
Minimum image size: 256×256 pixels
accuracy: 80–88% detection accuracy for identifying deconvolved images. Spectral flatness analysis alone achieves 75% accuracy. Combined with ringing detection, accuracy reaches 90% on uncompressed images. JPEG compression (quality < 85) reduces accuracy to 72%.
source: Cho, S. & Lee, S. (2009). Fast Motion Deblurring. ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH Asia), 28(5), Article 145.
useCase: Detecting when deconvolution or blind deblurring has been applied to AI-generated images to make them appear sharper. Identifying post-processing attempts to remove generation artifacts. Forensic analysis of sharpening history in disputed images.
strengths:
• Detects both blind and non-blind deconvolution traces
• Ringing artifacts are highly specific to deconvolution processing
• Spectral flatness provides a complementary, fast screening metric
• Effective at detecting Wiener, Richardson-Lucy, and total-variation deconvolution
• Can estimate the original blur kernel, providing forensic evidence of processing
limitations:
• Cannot distinguish deconvolution from aggressive unsharp masking in all cases
• JPEG compression artifacts can mask ringing patterns
• Very small deconvolution kernels (< 5×5) may not leave detectable traces
• Modern learned deconvolution networks (e.g., DeblurGAN) leave different, subtler traces
• Requires sufficient edge content in the image for ringing detection

references.title: Cho, S. & Lee, S. — Fast Motion Deblurring (SIGGRAPH Asia 2009)
Shan, Q., Jia, J., & Agarwala, A. — High-Quality Motion Deblurring from a Single Image (2008)
